Northern Iowa enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 23-12 overall after winning the Missouri Valley Conference tournament, and the Panthers finished the regular season 19-12 with an 11-9 MVC record before adding four Arch Madness wins. UNI closed league play by beating Drake 75-53 on March 1, 2026, a result the school’s recap explicitly said left the Panthers at 19-12 overall and 11-9 in conference play; the MVC title-game recap then said the UIC win pushed them to 23-12. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/news/2026/3/1/mens-basketball-uni-mens-basketball-cruises-to-75-53-win-at-drake))

Offensively, this is still a very traditional Ben Jacobson team: multiple-ballhandler half-court execution, heavy use of inside-out touches, and an emphasis on spacing that produces catch-and-shoot threes rather than chaos. The numbers back that up. UNI averaged 69.9 points per game, shot 47.7% from the field, 35.5% from three, and posted 526 assists against only 326 turnovers in 35 games, a strong 1.61 assist-to-turnover ratio. Trey Campbell is the organizing piece with 135 assists against 71 turnovers, while Max Weisbrod adds 61 assists and Ben Schwieger 66, so their offense is not one-creator dependent. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

The specific tendencies show up game to game. Against Evansville in the MVC opener on March 6, UNI assisted on nine of 12 made baskets in the first half, a clear sign of scripted half-court execution and drive-kick ball movement. Against Murray State on February 9, the recap noted the Panthers “attacked the paint,” then used a quick 5-0 burst with a Kyle Pock three and a Trey Campbell-Hornseth connection before halftime; that is the exact Jacobson formula, paint pressure first, perimeter spacing second. In the February 6 win over Bradley, UNI’s “interior game came to life in the second half” with 18 paint points, led by Will Hornseth and Trey Campbell. In the March 1 win at Drake, the Panthers “continued to attack the paint” even after Drake cut the margin, which is a useful indicator that they do not abandon structure late. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/news/2026/3/6/mens-basketball-uni-mens-basketball-outlasts-evansville-in-arch-madness-opener?utm_source=openai))

Personnel defines the sets. Hornseth is their most efficient finisher at 60.4% from the field and averages 11.2 points in only 26.4 minutes, which makes him the obvious dive man and short-roll target. Tristan Smith, at 55.5% shooting and 5.1 rebounds per game, gives them another paint scorer and interior passer option. Campbell leads the team at 13.7 points and 3.9 assists, so late-clock possessions often end with him in ball-screen creation or shot-making mode. Schwieger, at 9.9 points and 37.6% from three, and Weisbrod, with 55 made threes, are the spacing pieces around that core. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Defensively, UNI’s identity is clearer than its offense: control the game, guard the arc, finish possessions, and avoid fouling itself into unstable games. The team allowed only 61.3 points per game across 35 contests, and opponent shooting sits at 40.7% overall and 28.5% from three. On January 12, the school’s preview for UIC said Northern Iowa led Division I in three-point percentage defense at 25.7%, and on January 9 its Bradley preview said UNI ranked second nationally at 25.4%. Even if that national rank moved slightly over the season, the philosophy did not: shrink the floor, chase shooters off rhythm, and make opponents score over size at the rim. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Specific examples reinforce the scheme. In the March 7 quarterfinal against Illinois State, UNI held the Redbirds to 15% from three and 52 total points. In the March 1 road win at Drake, the Panthers forced 15 turnovers and held Drake to 31% shooting. In the February 6 win over Bradley, they forced 16 turnovers and turned that into 30 points off takeaways. In the January 24 win over Murray State, UNI’s “best-in-the-league scoring defense” held the MVC’s top scoring offense to its season-low in conference play, 76 points. This is not a gambling defense in the modern pressure sense; it is a positional defense that wins with closeouts, help timing, and selective ball pressure. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/news/2026/3/7/mens-basketball-panther-mens-basketball-rolls-into-mvc-semifinals-with-victory-of-redbirds))

Jacobson’s coaching philosophy remains pragmatic and visibly adjustment-based. One documented example came on January 24 against first-place Murray State: after a five-game losing streak, UNI changed the texture of the game by leaning harder into paint scoring and physical defense, winning 81-76 while Campbell scored a season-high 27. Another came against Bradley on February 6, when the recap explicitly noted the interior game “came to life in the second half,” evidence of a halftime adjustment away from a perimeter-stalled first half. A third came March 7 against Bradley in St. Louis: UNI built a 45-32 halftime lead by outshooting the Braves, then survived the second-half rally with key RJ Taylor shotmaking and enough composure to close 73-69. Jacobson’s teams also show pattern-level adjustment capacity; UNI was 18-1 when leading at halftime after the title game, which suggests the staff consistently protects advantages once it identifies what is working. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/news/2026/1/24/mens-basketball-uni-mens-basketball-takes-down-first-place-racers-at-home))

Clutch execution is a real strength, though not a flawless one. The best example is March 7 versus Bradley: UNI led big, got pushed, then answered with Taylor’s late three and held on for a 73-69 semifinal win. The March 8 title game was less dramatic but still a pressure performance; UNI shot 67.9% in the first half and never trailed for more than 34 seconds total in the entire MVC tournament, which is elite poise over four days. Earlier in the season, the Panthers beat Murray State 81-76 on January 24 to snap a five-game skid, and that game revealed shot-making under pressure from Campbell. They also had close-game failures that matter for scouting: a 91-86 loss at Belmont on February 12, a 59-57 home loss to Southern Illinois on February 21 when a tying layup missed at the buzzer, and a 71-69 home loss to Illinois State on February 25 after Hornseth gave UNI a 69-68 lead with 23 seconds left before the Redbirds answered with the winner. That resume says UNI can execute late, but if the opponent can force them into reactive half-court possessions, their margin narrows quickly. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/news/2026/3/7/mens-basketball-uni-mens-basketball-holds-off-bradley-to-advance-to-arch-madness-championship?utm_source=openai))

The key players are well defined. Campbell is the lead guard and emotional center: 13.7 points, 3.8 rebounds, 3.9 assists, 57 steals, and 34.7% from three over 35 starts. His standout moments include 27 points against Murray State on January 24, 13 points and six assists against Bradley in the MVC semifinal, and MVC Tournament MVP honors after the title run. Leon Bond III is the slashing wing scorer at 11.9 points and 4.8 rebounds; he scored 19 against Illinois State in the quarterfinal and another 19 on 7-of-8 shooting against Bradley in the semifinal. Hornseth is the efficient interior finisher at 11.2 points on 60.4% shooting, and he swung games with paint scoring, including a strong second half against Bradley on February 6 and a brief late lead against Illinois State on February 25. Schwieger gives balance with 9.9 points, 4.6 rebounds, and 35 made threes, including 17 points in the January 1 comeback win over Indiana State. Tristan Smith adds 9.1 points and 5.1 rebounds on 55.5% shooting, and he poured in 10 second-half points at Drake on March 1. Weisbrod is the designated floor spacer with 55 made threes and 38.7% accuracy from deep. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

The notable wins tell you what Northern Iowa looks like when the game is on its terms. The 81-76 win over first-place Murray State on January 24 showed UNI can beat high-end league offense by controlling paint touches and making Campbell the best creator on the floor. The 75-53 road win at Drake on March 1 showed top-end defensive ceiling: 15 forced turnovers and 31% opponent shooting. The MVC tournament wins over Bradley (73-69) and UIC (84-69) showed tournament composure and shot quality under pressure. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/news/2026/1/24/mens-basketball-uni-mens-basketball-takes-down-first-place-racers-at-home))

The notable losses reveal the pressure points. Belmont beat UNI twice in league play, including 91-86 on February 12, which suggests Northern Iowa can be vulnerable when the opponent has enough skill to stretch its shell and win a scoring game. Southern Illinois won 59-57 on February 21 in a grinder, showing that if UNI has to chase late in a low-possession game, it can run out of shot creation. Illinois State’s 71-69 win on February 25 showed another issue: even after a scorching second half and seven straight made threes, UNI could not get the final stop. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/sports/mbball/opponent-history/belmont-university/197?utm_source=openai))

Jacobson’s NCAA tournament history is substantial and relevant. UNI’s March 8 title-game recap states that 2026 is the program’s ninth NCAA berth and that Jacobson has a 5-1 record in MVC title games. Under Jacobson, Northern Iowa reached the 2010 Sweet 16 after beating UNLV and No. 1 seed Kansas, the 2015 Round of 32 after beating Wyoming, and the 2016 Round of 32 after beating Texas before losing to Texas A&M. His earlier UNI teams also reached the NCAA field in 2009 and 2022? No — for accuracy, the school’s official recap lists Jacobson-era NCAA berths in 2010, 2015, 2016, and now 2026, while the program also made pre-Jacobson trips in 1990, 2004, 2005, and 2006. So Jacobson’s documented NCAA round history as head coach is: Sweet 16 in 2010; Round of 32 in 2015; Round of 32 in 2016; and entering 2026 with the new bid secured. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/news/2026/3/8/mens-basketball-panther-mens-basketball-tops-uic-for-arch-madness-championship))

Bottom line: Northern Iowa is a classic Jacobson tournament team — disciplined, low-turnover, excellent at defending the arc, and old enough in the backcourt to stay functional in pressure possessions. The Panthers are not explosive by national standards at 69.9 points per game, but if Campbell controls tempo, Bond gets downhill, and Hornseth/Smith win the paint, they are dangerous because they can drag a higher-seeded opponent into a possession game and make every rotation matter. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Northern Iowa enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with a profile that is stronger in predictive metrics than in résumé metrics, and that distinction matters. The Panthers were 22-12 against Division I competition and arrived in the field on a five-game winning streak, including the Missouri Valley tournament title run. Their résumé sat in the at-large gray zone, but the underlying power numbers painted them as a credible top-75 team nationally rather than a fringe top-100 team. WarrenNolan’s ranking comparison page listed Northern Iowa at NET No. 72, ESPN BPI No. 82, KenPom No. 72, and Bart Torvik T-Rank No. 70 as of games through March 15, 2026. The same comparison page showed a major gap between predictive and result-based measures: KPI No. 77, but SOR No. 105 and WAB No. 101. In other words, the Panthers looked more like a solid team than a high-quality résumé. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/compare-rankings))

That split is reinforced by schedule context. Northern Iowa’s overall strength of schedule was only modest, with WarrenNolan listing SOS No. 114 on the team page and NET SOS No. 137 with non-conference NET SOS No. 195 on the NCAA-style team sheet. Their non-conference slate was not terrible by mid-major standards — WarrenNolan listed non-conference SOS No. 53 and non-conference RPI No. 57 — but the full-season schedule still did not provide many elite opportunities. The Panthers went 0-2 in Quadrant 1, 4-5 in Quadrant 2, 7-5 in Quadrant 3, and 11-0 in Quadrant 4. That is a classic profile of a team that took care of business against weaker opposition but did not accumulate enough top-end wins to lift the résumé into the tournament’s upper middle class. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-clubhouse?team=Northern-Iowa))

The cleanest statistical identity available in the public 2026 data is that Northern Iowa wins with defense, ball security, and shot selection discipline rather than with raw scoring volume. College Sports Madness’ tournament capsule, with stats through March 8, listed the Panthers at just 69.9 points per game, only 308th nationally, but 61.3 points allowed per game, tied for No. 1 nationally. That same capsule had them at 47.7% from the field, 35.5% from three, and only 9.3 turnovers per game, which ranked 14th nationally. They also allowed just 40.7% shooting overall, 30th nationally. So even without a fully accessible public KenPom component page, the available data strongly indicates a low-possession, low-mistake, defense-first team whose per-game scoring looks mediocre largely because the game environment is compressed. ([collegesportsmadness.com](https://www.collegesportsmadness.com/article/25108))

The possession-adjusted estimate that is available publicly supports that reading. WarrenNolan’s 2026 net rating page listed Northern Iowa with a net rating of +11.2, tied around 47th nationally. That is materially better than their NET and much better than their SOR/WAB standing, which implies the Panthers’ efficiency margin was stronger than their résumé. Because net rating is offensive rating minus defensive rating, a +11.2 mark suggests a team that was comfortably positive on both ends and likely better defensively than offensively. Given the publicly available capsule stats — elite scoring defense, strong field-goal defense, and extremely low turnover rate on offense — the most plausible adjusted-efficiency story is that Northern Iowa fielded a good-but-not-elite offense and a clearly high-level defense. Public search results did not expose an exact 2026 adjusted offense or adjusted defense figure from KenPom or Torvik, so the best evidence-based synthesis is: likely around top-70 nationally on offense, but closer to top-30 or better on defense, with the defense driving the overall profile. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-net-rating))

Shot profile clues are similarly suggestive even where exact tempo-free component rates were not openly accessible. Northern Iowa averaged 7.8 made threes per game and shot 35.5% from deep, good but not hyper-voluminous. Their offense was efficient enough in raw field-goal percentage at 47.7%, and they generated 15.0 assists per game while rarely giving the ball away. That usually maps to a structured half-court attack that values execution over pace. Their free-throw percentage was only 69.9%, however, and their rebound margin was -1.1, so this was not a team steamrolling opponents with physical dominance. The likely hidden truth in the Four Factors is that Northern Iowa’s offensive TO% was excellent, their eFG% was solid, their OR% was probably mediocre at best, and their FT rate probably was not a major strength. Put differently: they won possessions by not wasting them, not by overwhelming teams on the glass or constantly living at the line. ([collegesportsmadness.com](https://www.collegesportsmadness.com/article/25108))

Recent form is one of the strongest parts of the profile. WarrenNolan listed Northern Iowa at 7-3 over its last 10 games and on a 5-game winning streak entering the NCAA field. The game log on the NET team sheet shows that run included neutral-floor wins over Illinois State, 74-52, and Bradley, 73-69, plus the MVC title-game win over UIC, 84-69. Just before that, they also won at Drake, 75-53, and at Indiana State, 81-60. That is meaningful because it suggests the Panthers’ March version was better than the aggregate résumé. The offense in particular appears to have spiked late: 84 against UIC, 73 against Bradley, 75 at Drake, 81 at Indiana State. For a team whose season-long scoring average was under 70, that closing stretch hints at offensive improvement without sacrificing the defense-first template. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-clubhouse?team=Northern-Iowa))

The divergence from conventional wisdom is pretty clear. A casual observer looking only at 69.9 points per game might tag Northern Iowa as offensively limited and generally mediocre. The deeper numbers disagree. Predictive systems clustered them around 70-82 nationally, not around 100+, and the net-rating number of +11.2 was even more flattering. Their issue was not that they were bad; it was that they played a style that depressed scoring, faced only a middling schedule, and lacked marquee wins. The eye test may say “grindy mid-major with limited ceiling.” The analytics say “competent tournament team with strong defensive habits, elite turnover avoidance, and an efficiency margin better than its résumé.” That makes Northern Iowa a dangerous draw in the specific tournament sense: they are unlikely to beat themselves, they can drag higher-seeded teams into a half-court game, and their statistical floor is higher than people expect from a No. 72 NET auto-bid. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/compare-rankings))

Bottom line: Northern Iowa’s 2026 tournament profile is built on defensive resistance, possession control, and late-season stabilization. The Panthers were not an explosive offense and probably were not elite in offensive rebounding or free-throw generation, but they defended at a nationally relevant level, protected the ball at an exceptional rate, shot well enough to stay efficient, and entered March playing their best basketball. The résumé says lower-tier tournament team; the predictive metrics say they are materially more competent than that label implies. ([collegesportsmadness.com](https://www.collegesportsmadness.com/article/25108))
matchup-analyst:
Northern Iowa enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a classic Ben Jacobson team: very slow, very physical, and extremely comfortable playing in the half court. Their season profile is blunt. UNI averages 69.9 points per game, shoots 47.7% from the field, 35.5% from three, and commits only 9.3 turnovers per game; RotoWire, citing KenPom, lists the Panthers with the nation’s second-lowest adjusted tempo and a 13.24% offensive turnover rate. That combination tells you exactly what they want: long possessions, low-possession games, and shot quality without giveaways. Trey Campbell is the primary organizer at 13.7 points and 3.9 assists per game, while the frontcourt scoring is spread among Will Hornseth (11.2 ppg, 60.4% FG), Leon Bond III (11.9 ppg), Ben Schwieger (9.9 ppg), and Tristan Smith (9.1 ppg). ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2460))

**Style of play and what disrupts it:** UNI’s offense is not built around high-volume individual creation; it is built around execution, screening, interior touches to Hornseth/Smith, and complementary shooting from Campbell, Weisbrod, Bond, and Schwieger. The assist totals support that: Campbell has 135 assists, Hornseth 76, Schwieger 66, Weisbrod 61, and Smith 51, which is a lot of shared creation for a 35-game sample. Their preferred offensive environment is deliberate and organized. The tactics that have disrupted them this year are physical ball pressure that delays entry into sets, aggressive gap help that shrinks the lane without surrendering clean catch-and-shoot rhythm, and lineups that can both switch forward actions and recover to shooters. In the Jan. 13 home loss to UIC, UNI was outscored 13-3 off turnovers and “was held without a three-point basket in the final frame.” In the Jan. 28 loss at Southern Illinois, a season-high 17 turnovers “plagued” UNI, including 10 in the second half, and SIU got transition offense off missed layups and giveaways. In the Jan. 21 loss at Illinois State, UNI scored a season-low 16 first-half points and shot just 27% in the first half, a sign that early-clock disruption and physicality can freeze their offense before it gets into second and third actions. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/news/2026/1/13/mens-basketball-uni-mens-basketball-drops-home-matchup-to-uic))

**Press and zone vulnerability:** The best hard evidence of press vulnerability is turnover response. UNI is normally elite at ball security, but the games where opponents raised pressure and length are the clearest stress points. UIC’s March 8 title-game recap explicitly noted “increased defensive pressure from the Flames,” even in a UNI win; the difference is that UNI answered that pressure with 84 points, six threes from Campbell, and dominant defensive rebounding. Earlier, on Jan. 13, UIC’s pressure was more effective: 11 UNI turnovers, 13-3 deficit in points off turnovers, and no made second-half threes. Southern Illinois also forced 17 turnovers on Jan. 28 and 18 more on Feb. 21 even though UNI nearly stole that one late. That is enough evidence to say pressure can bother them if it is attached to length and if it turns into live-ball conversion chances. There is not strong public game-log evidence that a zone alone has solved UNI; the stronger conclusion from the available 2026 evidence is that pressure-plus-shrunk driving lanes has hurt them more than static zone. If you zone them, it has to be an active matchup zone with hard stunts at Campbell and early tags on Hornseth, because UNI has multiple 35%+ perimeter pieces and went 10-for-25 from three at Drake, 54.5% from deep in the second half there. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/news/2026/3/8/mens-basketball-panther-mens-basketball-tops-uic-for-arch-madness-championship?utm_source=openai))

**Preferred pace and how to force the opposite:** UNI wants a 60- to low-60s-possession game. RotoWire/KenPom’s note that they have the nation’s second-slowest adjusted tempo is the macro proof, and their own tournament note says their “offensive pace, paired with elite defense” fueled late improvement, which in context still means deliberate offense rather than transition volume. To force the opposite, you must create pace without gifting them spot-up threes: score before their half-court defense sets, push off misses, and especially run after their turnovers. Southern Illinois provides the cleanest example; the Salukis “thrived in transition off missed Northern Iowa layups” in a 65-50 win. Belmont provides the opposite lesson: it sped the game up to a 91-86 scoreline and shot 57% from the floor while making nine first-half threes. If you can make UNI defend multiple early-clock actions and cross-matches, you can drag them away from the low-possession grinder they prefer. ([rotowire.com](https://www.rotowire.com/cbasketball/team/northern-iowa-1544?utm_source=openai))

**Size and athleticism mismatches by position:** At lead guard, Campbell is 6-4, 195 and gives UNI unusual size for a primary handler. Smaller point guards will struggle to bother his vision unless they have elite quickness or trap support. At the other guard spot, Max Weisbrod is also 6-4, 190 and functions as a spacing guard; bigger, more explosive wings can attack him off the bounce, but helping off him is dangerous because he made 55 threes at 38.7%. On the wing/forward line, Bond is 6-5, 200 and the best straight-line athlete in the main rotation, while Schwieger is 6-8, 220 and Hornseth is 6-8, 235. That gives UNI real positional size at the 3/4/5 spots. Tristan Smith, at 6-6, 235, is strong but undersized as a true interior anchor, so long 6-10 or 6-11 finishers can shoot over him, while quick face-up 4s can drag him away from the rim. Hornseth is the most efficient interior scorer at 60.4% FG and also a connective passer with 76 assists, but his 53.5% FT can be targeted late. The main athletic mismatch against UNI is not raw size at the 2-4 spots; it is high-major vertical pop at the 5 and burst at the point of attack. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/roster/_/id/2460/northern-iowa-panthers))

**Isolation vs. team offense tendencies:** Publicly available 2026 team data strongly indicates UNI is a team-offense group, not an isolation-heavy one. Their top scorer, Campbell, averages 3.9 assists, and five rotation players have at least 51 assists. As a team they average 15.0 assists per game against only 9.3 turnovers, a 1.61 assist/turnover ratio. RotoWire’s team page lists a 13.24% offensive turnover rate, reinforcing that they value possession quality and collective creation. I do not have a reliable primary-source 2026 Synergy play-type split that gives exact isolation frequency percentage versus set offense percentage, so I will not invent one. The available evidence supports this narrower, supportable claim: UNI is overwhelmingly a read-and-react, pass-connected half-court offense rather than a pure one-on-one offense. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2460))

**Transition offense and defense frequency:** I do not have a reliable primary-source 2026 possession-frequency table for exact transition offense/defense percentages, so I cannot responsibly give a numeric frequency split. What is supportable is that transition is not their preferred offensive identity, while transition defense can become vulnerable when their offense breaks structure. In the Drake win, UNI scored only 9 fast-break points but crushed Drake with half-court efficiency, 26 points off turnovers, and 36 paint points. In the Southern Illinois road loss, the recap explicitly says SIU “thrived in transition off missed Northern Iowa layups,” which is the exact blueprint for stressing UNI’s retreat defense. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26/drake/boxscore/8160))

**Coaching adaptability:** Ben Jacobson’s staff showed real in-season adaptability in the clearest possible way: Northern Iowa lost five straight in January, scoring only 58.6 points per game on 37.8% shooting during that skid, then entered Arch Madness having won seven of 11 and eventually won four games in four days to claim the MVC title. Specific game evidence backs that up. UNI lost to UIC at home on Jan. 13, then beat UIC 84-69 in the MVC final on March 8 with Campbell drilling six threes. UNI also lost at Southern Illinois on Jan. 28 and then, in the Feb. 21 rematch, forced 18 Saluki turnovers and nearly erased an 11-point late deficit before losing 59-57. That is not a literal playoff “series,” but it is strong evidence of rematch adjustment within the season. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/news/2026/3/3/mens-basketball-uni-mens-basketball-opens-arch-madness-play-thursday-night-in-st-louis))

**Concrete game plan — To beat this team you must:** 1) Pick up Campbell early and make the first action start 5-7 feet farther from the arc; UIC and SIU disrupted UNI when the Panthers were forced into late-clock offense and turnovers. 2) Load the lane against Hornseth and Smith, but close under control to Weisbrod and Campbell; UNI is efficient inside, but its losses often feature poor early offense and scoring droughts. 3) Run after every live-ball turnover and every missed layup; Southern Illinois beat them this way. 4) Attack Smith with length and Hornseth with quickness; those are the cleanest frontcourt mismatch points. 5) Do not let the game become a half-court chess match at 62 possessions; Belmont’s 91-86 win and SIU’s transition success are better templates than trying to out-grind Jacobson. 6) If leading late, foul Hornseth before the bonus gets too deep if matchup and game context allow; he is at 53.5% from the line. 7) On defense, mix man with a matchup zone or soft press not because zone alone will beat them, but because changing the picture can chew clock and keep Campbell from walking into organized actions. That is the formula: extend pressure, win the first 10 seconds of the possession, turn misses and miscues into pace, and force UNI’s skilled but methodical frontcourt to play from behind on the scoreboard. ([unipanthers.com](https://unipanthers.com/news/2026/1/28/mens-basketball-panther-mens-basketball-falls-at-southern-illinois))
